questions.question_text:
A coin is tossed $40$ times and lands on Heads $22$ times.
What is the experimental probability of obtaining Heads, as a decimal?

options.why: States the theoretical probability instead of calculating the experimental relative frequency.
Calculates the experimental probability of Tails ($18/40 = 0.45$) instead of Heads.
Converts the frequency count of $22$ directly to a decimal without dividing by $40$.

questions.question_text: According to the Law of Large Numbers, what happens to the relative frequency of an outcome as the number of experimental trials increases?

options.text: It approaches the true theoretical probability.
It fluctuates with increasingly large swings away from the theoretical probability.
options.why: Typical random variability diminishes as the sample size grows, although actual fluctuations need not decrease at every trial.

options.text: It becomes exactly equal to $0.5$ for every possible random experiment.
options.why: Relative frequency approaches the specific event's theoretical probability, not necessarily $0.5$.

options.text: It increases continually until it equals $1.0$ at very large numbers of trials.
options.why: Probabilities sum to $1$, but an individual event's probability does not grow to $1$.

questions.solution_text: As trials increase, relative frequency approaches the theoretical probability. It need not get closer after every trial.

questions.question_text:
In a quality test of $180$ electronic components, $12$ were defective.
What is the estimated probability that a component is defective, correct to $2$ decimal places?

options.why: Divides the count $12$ by $100$ instead of the total $180$.
Calculates the relative frequency of non-defective components: $168/180 \approx 0.93$.
Truncates $0.0666\ldots$ to two decimal places instead of rounding.

questions.question_text:
A six-sided die is rolled $150$ times and lands on '3' on $33$ rolls.
What is the relative frequency of rolling a '3', as a decimal?

options.why: Divides $33$ by $100$ instead of $150$.
Calculates the relative frequency of outcomes other than '3': $117/150 = 0.78$.
Doubles the trial count before dividing: $33/300 = 0.11$.

questions.question_text:
Survey 1 polls $25$ voters and finds $60\%$ support a policy.
Survey 2 polls $1000$ voters and finds $52\%$ support the policy.
Assume both surveys use comparable sampling methods for the same population under stable conditions. Why is Survey 2's result generally more reliable as an estimate of the true population proportion?

options.text: A larger sample size significantly reduces random sampling variability.
Because a $52\%$ support rate is always more accurate than a $60\%$ support rate.
options.why: The value of the percentage does not determine reliability; the sample size does.

options.text: Because Survey 1 had too high a percentage to be statistically possible.
options.why: $60\%$ is a perfectly valid percentage; sample size is the issue.

options.text: Because smaller surveys never reflect any true population opinions.
options.why: Small surveys provide estimates, but with higher margin of error rather than zero value.

questions.solution_text:
Larger sample sizes reduce random sampling variability and provide more reliable estimates.
A larger sample size significantly reduces random sampling variability.

questions.question_text:
A survey of $250$ students finds $65$ travel by bicycle, $85$ by bus, and $100$ by car.
What is the estimated probability that a randomly chosen student travels by bicycle?

options.why: Calculates the probability of bus travel: $85 / 250 = 0.34$.
Calculates the probability of car travel: $100 / 250 = 0.40$.
Converts the frequency $65$ directly into a decimal without dividing by $250$.

questions.question_text:
A spinner with four colours was spun $120$ times, landing on Yellow $42$ times.
What is the estimated probability of Yellow?

options.why: Assumes the four colours are equally likely instead of using the observed frequency.
Divides $42$ by $100$ instead of $120$.
Calculates the relative frequency of results other than Yellow: $78/120 = 0.65$.

questions.question_text:
An experiment records these outcome frequencies:
$\begin{array}{c|c} \text{Outcome} & \text{Frequency} \\ \hline 14 & 137 \\ 15 & 211 \\ 16 & 189 \\ 17 & 163 \end{array}$
What is the relative frequency of outcome $15$, correct to $2$ decimal places?

options.why: Uses the frequency of all other outcomes: $489/700 \approx 0.70$.
Uses the frequency of outcome $16$: $189/700 = 0.27$.
Excludes outcome $15$ from the denominator: $211/489 \approx 0.43$.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{Total frequency} = 137 + 211 + 189 + 163 = 700$
$\text{Relative frequency of } 15 = \frac{211}{700} = 0.301428\ldots$
$\approx 0.30$ to $2$ decimal places.
